title: GM crops, twenty-five years on

turns.speaker: Cass
turns.text: The new rules split gene editing from transgenics. Editing gets treated like conventional breeding, more or less.

turns.speaker: Femi
turns.text: Which is scientifically defensible. Editing changes a gene the plant already has. It's what breeders have done slowly for ten thousand years.

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: The safety case was never really the sticking point though, was it. Twenty-five years of eating it and nothing has shown up.

turns.speaker: Cass
turns.text: No. The objection that stuck was about ownership.

turns.speaker: Femi
turns.text: Patented seed, contracts forbidding saving it, and a handful of companies controlling the whole chain.

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: Which is a real objection and it was consistently answered as if people were worried about their health.

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: So the debate talked past itself for two decades.

turns.speaker: Cass
turns.text: The herbicide point matters too. A lot of the first generation was engineered to survive spraying, so usage went up rather than down.

turns.speaker: Femi
turns.text: Fair, although the insect-resistant varieties cut insecticide substantially. It depends entirely which trait you mean.

turns.speaker: Cass
turns.text: Which is why arguing about GM as one thing never worked.

turns.speaker: Ingrid
turns.text: Does editing change the ownership problem at all?

turns.speaker: Femi
turns.text: In principle yes, because it's cheap enough for a university or a national programme to do. In practice the patents are already being filed.

turns.speaker: Cass
turns.text: So the technology got democratic and the law didn't.

points: New rules treat gene editing differently from transgenic modification, closer to conventional breeding.
Femi defends this scientifically, since editing alters genes the plant already has.
Ingrid notes safety was never the real objection, with no harm found after twenty-five years.
The durable objection concerns ownership: patented seed, contracts against saving it, and concentrated corporate control.
Cass notes herbicide-tolerant crops increased spraying, while Femi points out insect-resistant varieties cut insecticide, so the trait matters more than the category.
Femi expects editing to be cheap enough for public institutions, but patents are already being filed, so the technology became accessible while the law did not.
